## Back to the M&Ms

We talked about the binomial test for the proportion of orange M&Ms...but there are more than just orange and not-orange!

## Learning goals

1. Analyze a single categorical variable with >2 categories using the [$\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit test]{.alert}


## Fast facts

|           | **Binomial test of proportions**  | **$\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit test** |
|-----------------------|-----------------------|-----------------------------------|
| Number of variables   | 1                     | 1                     |
| Type of data          | categorical **(2 categories)** | categorical **(>2 categories)** |
| Parameter             | $p$                   | $\vec{p}$                   |
| Estimate              | $\hat{p}$             | $\vec{\hat{p}}$             |
| Sampling distribution | Binomial distribution | $\chi^2$ distribution |
| Test statistic        | Number of "successes" | $\chi^2$ statistic |

::: {.fragment .fade-out}
::: {style="width: 500px; height: 700px; background-color: white; border: 2px solid white; position: absolute; top: 50px; left: 600px; z-index: 999;"}
:::
:::

## [$\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit test]{.alert}

> The [$\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit test]{.alert} compares frequency data to a probabiity model stated by the null hypothesis

## M&M colors

According to Mars Chocolate North America, there are 210 candies in a 7 oz. bag and the proportion of M&M colors are:

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}

 Color  | Proportion
--------|:----------:
 Blue   | 0.24
 Orange | 0.20
 Green  | 0.16
 Yellow | 0.14
 Red    | 0.13
 Brown  | 0.13

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}




:::: {.r-stack}

::::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index="1"}
::: {.pause-think}
Suppose you want to test the hypothesis that the specific bag you have is unusual. What's a reasonable [null hypothesis]{.alert}?
:::
:::::

::::: {.fragment fragment-index="1"}
$H_0$: The frequency of M&Ms with each color in the bag is proportional to their proportion specified by the manufacturer

$H_\mathrm{A}$: The frequency of M&Ms with each color in the bag is ***not*** proportional to their proportion specified by the manufacturer
:::::

::::

:::
:::





## M&M colors

::: {.pause-think}
For a bag with 210 candies, what's the expected frequency of each color under $H_0$? ***A***, ***B***, or ***C***?
:::

```{r}
mm_expected <- tibble(
    Color = c("Blue", "Orange", "Green", "Yellow", "Red", "Brown"),
    Proportion = c("0.24", "0.20", "0.16", "0.14", "0.13", "0.13"),
    `Expected A` = rep(35, 6),
    `Expected B` = c(24, 20, 16, 14, 13, 13),
    `Expected C` = c("50.4", "42.0", "33.6", "29.4", "27.3", "27.3")
)

knitr::kable(mm_expected, align = "lcccc")
```

## M&M colors

The frequency of each color expected under $H_0$ is the proportion multiplied by the total number (e.g. $0.24 \times 210 = 50.4$)

```{r}
mm_expected <- select(mm_expected, c(Color, Proportion, `Expected C`)) |> 
    rename(Expected = `Expected C`) |> 
    rbind(c("**Total**", "1", "210"))

knitr::kable(mm_expected, align = "lcc")
```


## M&M colors

Now, take a random sample

```{r}
#| echo: true

candies <- sample(
    x = c("Blue", "Orange", "Green", "Yellow",
          "Red", "Brown"),
    size = 210,
    replace = TRUE,
    prob = c(0.24, 0.20, 0.16, 0.14, 0.13, 0.13)
)

table(candies)
```

::: {.fragment}
Think of this random sample as the bag we happen to "observe"
:::

## M&M colors

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="65%"}
```{r}
obs <- table(candies) |> 
    (function(x) {
        data.frame(Color = names(x), 
                   Observed = as.character(as.numeric(x)))
    })() |> 
    rbind(c("**Total**", "210")) |> 
    left_join(mm_expected, y = _)

obs$Observed[is.na(obs$Observed)] <- "0"

knitr::kable(obs, align = "lccc")
```

:::

::: {.column width="35%"}
::: {.fragment}
::: {.pause-think}
- Which color's observed frequency most deviates from expected?
- Do you think the observations are consistent with the null hypothesis?
:::
:::
:::
:::

## M&M colors

```{r}
chi <- mutate(obs, 
       o_min_e_raw = (as.numeric(Observed) - as.numeric(Expected)) |> 
           round(1),
       o_min_e = as.character(o_min_e_raw), 
       chi_sq_raw = (o_min_e_raw^2) / as.numeric(Expected), 
       chi_sq = round(chi_sq_raw, 2) |> 
           as.character())
chi$chi_sq[7] <- sum(chi$chi_sq_raw) |> 
    round(2) |> 
    as.character()

O <- round(as.numeric(chi$Observed))
E <- round(as.numeric(chi$Expected), 1)


chi_tab <- select(chi, c(Color:Observed, o_min_e, chi_sq)) |> 
    rename(`$O - E$` = o_min_e, 
           `$(O - E)^2/E$` = chi_sq) |> 
    kable(align = "lccccc")

chi_tab
```


## $\chi^2_i$ measures discrepancy between observed and expected frequency

$\chi^2_i$ for observation $i$ is

$$\chi^2_i = \frac{(Observed_i - Expected_i) ^ 2}{\mathit{Expected}_i}$$

Shorter form:

$$\chi^2_i = \frac{(O_i - E_i) ^ 2}{E_i}$$

## M&M colors

$$\chi^2_i = \frac{(O_i - E_i) ^ 2}{E_i} = \frac{(`r O[1]` - `r E[1]`)^2}{`r E[1]`} = `r round(((O[1] - E[1])^2) / E[1], 2)`$$

```{r}
chi_tab
```


## Why $\frac{(O_i - E_i) ^ 2}{E_i}$?

Positive and negative discrepancies have same magnitude: $(O_i - E_i) ^ 2$

Smaller $E_i$ have larger effect: $\frac{1}{E_i}$

 Proportion | Expected | Observed | $(O - E)^2 / E$
------------|----------|----------|-----------------
 0.5        | 50       | 40       | `r round((50 - 40)^2 / 50, 2)`
 0.2        | 20       | 30       | `r round((30 - 20)^2 / 20, 2)`
 0.2        | 20       | 10       | `r round((20 - 10)^2 / 20, 2)`
 0.1        | 10       | 20       | `r round((10 - 20)^2 / 10, 2)`

## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}

1. State $H_0$ and $H_\mathrm{A}$
2. Calculate the test statistic
3. Generate the null distribution
4. Calculate the $P$-value
6. Decide:
    - Reject $H_0$ if test statistic is $\ge$ critical value ($P \le \alpha$)
    - Fail to reject $H_0$ if test statistic is < critical value ($P > \alpha$)

## [$\chi^2$ statistic]{.alert}

> The [$\chi^2$]{.alert} statistic measures the discrepency between observed frequencies from the data and expected frequencies from the null hypothesis

[$\chi^2$ statistic]{.alert} is the test statistic for the [$\chi^2$]{.alert} test.

## [$\chi^2$ statistic]{.alert}

[$\chi^2$ statistic]{.alert} is calculated by summing up all $n$ $\chi^2_i$ values

$$\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \chi^2_i= \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(O_i - E_i) ^ 2}{E_i}$$

## M&M colors

 Color  | Proportion | Expected | Observed | $(O - E)^2 / E$
--------|:----------:|:--------:|:--------:|:---------------:
 Blue   | 0.24       | 50.4     | 43       | `r round((O[1] - E[1]) ^ 2 / E[1], 2)`
 Orange | 0.20       | 42.0     | 40       | `r round((O[2] - E[2]) ^ 2 / E[2], 2)`
 Green  | 0.16       | 33.6     | 37       | `r round((O[3] - E[3]) ^ 2 / E[3], 2)`
 Yellow | 0.14       | 29.4     | 37       | `r round((O[4] - E[4]) ^ 2 / E[4], 2)`
 Red    | 0.13       | 27.3     | 33       | `r round((O[5] - E[5]) ^ 2 / E[5], 2)`
 Brown  | 0.13       | 27.3     | 20       | `r round((O[6] - E[6]) ^ 2 / E[6], 2)`
 **Total**  | 1.00   | 210      | 210      | `r round(sum((O - E) ^ 2 / E), 2)`

::: {.pause-think}
What is the test statistic?
:::

## 

How often would we expect a discrepancy of $\ge `r round(sum((O - E) ^ 2 / E), 2)`$ under $H_0$?

## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}

1. State $H_0$ and $H_\mathrm{A}$
2. Calculate the test statistic
3. **Generate the null distribution** $\leftarrow$
4. Calculate the $P$-value
6. Decide:
    - Reject $H_0$ if test statistic is $\ge$ critical value ($P \le \alpha$)
    - Fail to reject $H_0$ if test statistic is < critical value ($P > \alpha$)

## [$\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert}

> The **[$\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert}** is the sampling distribution for $\chi^2$ test statistic

**Assumptions**

* None of the categories have an expected frequency of less than 1
* No more than 20% of the categories have expected frequencies less than 5

 Red    | 0.13       | 27.3

$\checkmark$ Under 20% of Expected values < 5

## [$\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert}

Under the null hypothesis, the more categories, the larger the test statistic



::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**3 categories**

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\chi^2 &= \sum_{i=1}^3 \frac{(O_i - E_i) ^ 2}{E_i} \\
&= \frac{(O_1 - E_1) ^ 2}{E_1} + \frac{(O_2 - E_2) ^ 2}{E_2} + \frac{(O_3 - E_3) ^ 2}{E_3}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**6 categories**

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\chi^2 = &\sum_{i=1}^6 \frac{(O_i - E_i) ^ 2}{E_i} \\
= &\frac{(O_1 - E_1) ^ 2}{E_1} + \frac{(O_2 - E_2) ^ 2}{E_2} + \frac{(O_3 - E_3) ^ 2}{E_3} + \\
&\frac{(O_4 - E_4) ^ 2}{E_4} + \frac{(O_5 - E_5) ^ 2}{E_5} + \frac{(O_6 - E_6) ^ 2}{E_6}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
:::
:::

## [Degrees of freedom for $\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert}

> The [degrees of freedom]{.alert} of a $\chi^2$ statistic capture this fact that more categories equates to larger values

$$df = \mathrm{(Number~of~categories)} - 1$$

## More [degrees of freedom]{.alert} = more likely to have larger values

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "8in"

df <- crossing(
    x = seq(0, 20, 0.01),
    df = c(2, 4, 8)
) |>
    mutate(y = dchisq(x, df), panel = str_c("df = ", df))

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
    facet_grid(rows = vars(panel)) +
    geom_area(fill = "tomato") +
    xlab(expression(chi^2~statistic)) +
    ylab("Probability density") +
    theme_cowplot() +
    scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 4)
```


## [Degrees of freedom]{.alert} depends on number of categories, not sample size

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
df <- tibble(
    Expected = c(60, 60, 60),
    Observed = c(57, 62, 61),
    `$\\chi^2_i$` = (Observed - Expected) ^ 2 / Expected
)

knitr::kable(df, escape = FALSE, align = rep("c", 3),
             digits = 3)

df$chisq <- df$`$\\chi^2_i$`
```

$$\mathit{df} = 3 - 1 = 2$$
$$
\begin{align}
\chi^2 &= `r str_c(round(df$chisq, 3), collapse = "+")` \\
&= `r round(sum(df$chisq), 3)`
\end{align}
$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
df <- tibble(
  Expected = c(600, 600, 600),
  Observed = c(570, 620, 610),
  `$\\chi^2_i$` = (Observed - Expected) ^ 2 / Expected
)

knitr::kable(df, escape = FALSE, align = rep("c", 3),
             digits = 3)

df$chisq <- df$`$\\chi^2_i$`
```

$$\mathit{df} = 3 - 1 = 2$$
$$
\begin{align}
\chi^2 &= `r str_c(round(df$chisq, 3), collapse = "+")` \\
&= `r round(sum(df$chisq), 3)`
\end{align}
$$
:::
:::

## $\chi_5^2$ distribution (graphically)

Read $\chi_5^2$ as "$\chi^2$ distribution with $d.f. = 2$"

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "10in"

df <- tibble(
    x = seq(0, 20, 0.01),
    y = dchisq(x, 5)
)

gp <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_area(fill = "tomato") +
    xlab(expression(chi^2~statistic)) +
    ylab("Probability density") +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(
        strip.text = element_text(size = 18),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 24),
        title = element_text(size = 24)
    )

gp
```



## $\chi_5^2$ distribution with test statistic




Recall we calculated for the M&Ms: $\chi^2 = `r chi[7, 8]`$

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "9.5in"

mm_test_stat <- sum((O - E) ^ 2 / E)

gp +
    geom_area(data = filter(df, x < mm_test_stat), fill = "white",
              size = 2, color = "tomato") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = mm_test_stat, size = 2)
```

## $\chi_\mathit{df}^2$ distribution


The $P$-value is the area to the right of test statistic.

So this is a [one-tailed]{.alert} test. Why?

We are only interested if the discrepancy between *Expected* and *Observed* is **more** than we expect under $H_0$

$$\frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i}$$

Higher test statistics = more discrepancy between *Expected* and *Observed*

## $\chi_\mathit{df}^2$ distribution

Why is the $\chi_\mathit{df}^2$ distribution *continuous* even though we are working with a categorical variable with discrete frequencies?

Because $\chi_\mathit{df}^2$ is an approximation of the "true" sampling distribution


## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}

1. State $H_0$ and $H_A$
2. Calculate the test statistic
3. Generate the null distribution
5. ***Calculate the P-value*** $\leftarrow$
6. Decide:
    - Reject $H_0$ if the P-value is less than or equal to $\alpha$ ($P \le \alpha$)
    - Fail to reject $H_0$ if P-value is greater than $\alpha$ ($P > \alpha$)

## [$P$-value]{.alert}

$\chi^2~\text{statistic} = `r sum((O - E) ^ 2 / E)`$, $\mathit{df} = 5$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

cat(sprintf("```r\npchisq(q = %s,\n       df = 5,\n       lower.tail = FALSE)\n```", 
            round(mm_test_stat, 7)))
```

```{r}
pchisq(q = x2,
       df = 5,
       lower.tail = FALSE)
```

::: {.fragment}
*(Note: if you were alive in the Pleistocene you might look up a P-value value in a table in the back of your stats book)*
:::



## Decide

```{r}
p_value <- pchisq(mm_test_stat, df = 5, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

::: {.incremental}
- $\alpha = 0.05$
- $P = `r round(p_value, 2)`$
- $`r round(p_value, 2)` > 0.05$
:::

::: {.fragment}
We fail to reject $H_0$

We do not have sufficient evidence to say that the frequency of candy colors differs significantly from what we would expect based on the manufacturer's information
:::

## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}

1. State $H_0$ and $H_\mathrm{A}$
2. Calculate the test statistic
3. Generate the null distribution
4. ***Find the [critical value]{.alert} at a specified $\alpha$***
6. Decide:
    - Reject $H_0$ if test statistic is $\ge$ critical value (same as $P \le \alpha$)
    - Fail to reject $H_0$ if test statistic is < critical value (same as $P > \alpha$)

## [Critical value]{.alert}

> A [critical value]{.alert} is the value of a test statistic that marks the boundary of a specified area in the tail (or tails) of the sampling distribution under $H_0$

## [Critical value]{.alert}

You *can* look up critical values in a table if you're a dinosaur

$\alpha = 0.05$, $\mathit{df} = 5$

```{r}
#| echo: true

qchisq(0.05,
       df = 5,
       lower.tail = FALSE)
```

## $\chi_5^2$ distribution with critical value

$\alpha = 0.05$, $\mathit{df} = 5$

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "9in"

mm_crit_stat <- qchisq(0.05, 5, lower.tail = FALSE)

gp +
  geom_area(data = filter(df, x < mm_crit_stat), fill = "white",
            size = 2, color = "tomato") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mm_crit_stat, size = 2, linetype = "dashed")
```

## $\chi_5^2$ distribution with critical value

$\alpha = 0.05$, $\mathit{df} = 5$

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "9in"

mm_crit_stat <- qchisq(0.05, 5, lower.tail = FALSE)

gp +
  geom_area(data = filter(df, x < mm_test_stat), fill = "white",
            size = 2, color = "tomato") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mm_test_stat, size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mm_crit_stat, size = 2, linetype = "dashed")
```


## The quick way in *R*

```{r}
#| echo: true

chisq.test(x = c(43, 40, 37, 37, 33, 20),
           p = c(0.24, 0.20, 0.16, 0.14, 0.13, 0.13))
```

## Summary

The [$\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert} describes the sampling distribution of the discrepancy between expected and observed frequencies

It is an approximate test, but works well when sample size are large that assumptions are met

## Learning Objectives

1. Analyze two or more categorical variable with $\ge 2$ categories using the [$\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert} and [contingency analysis]{.alert}

## Review of $\chi^2$ goodness of fit test

|           | **$\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit test** |
|-----------------------|-----------------------|
| Number of variables   | 1                     |
| Type of data          | categorical **(>2 categories)** |
| Parameter             | $\vec{p}$             |
| Estimate              | $\vec{\hat{p}}$       |
| Sampling distribution | $\chi^2$ distribution |
| Test statistic        | $\chi^2$ statistic    |

## [$\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit test]{.alert}

> The [$\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit test]{.alert} compares frequency data to a probability model stated by the null hypothesis

## M&M colors

```{r}
E <- 210 * c(0.24, 0.20, 0.16, 0.14, 0.13, 0.13)
O <- c(43, 40, 37, 37, 33, 20)
```

 Color  | Proportion | Expected | Observed | $(O - E)^2 / E$
--------|------------|----------|----------|-----------------
 Blue   | 0.24       | 50.4     | 43       | `r round((O[1] - E[1]) ^ 2 / E[1], 2)`
 Orange | 0.20       | 42.0     | 40       | `r round((O[2] - E[2]) ^ 2 / E[2], 2)`
 Green  | 0.16       | 33.6     | 37       | `r round((O[3] - E[3]) ^ 2 / E[3], 2)`
 Yellow | 0.14       | 29.4     | 37       | `r round((O[4] - E[4]) ^ 2 / E[4], 2)`
 Red    | 0.13       | 27.3     | 33       | `r round((O[5] - E[5]) ^ 2 / E[5], 2)`
 Brown  | 0.13       | 27.3     | 20       | `r round((O[6] - E[6]) ^ 2 / E[6], 2)`
 **Total**  | 1.00   | 210      | 210

$$\chi^2_i = \frac{(Observed_i - Expected_i) ^ 2}{\mathit{Expected}_i}$$

$\chi^2_i$ measures discrepancy between observed and expected frequency

## [$\chi^2$ statistic]{.alert}

> The [$\chi^2$]{.alert} statistic measures the discrepency between observed frequencies from the data and expected frequencies from the null hypothesis

[$\chi^2$ statistic]{.alert} is calculated by summing up all $n$ $\chi^2_i$ values

$$\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \chi^2_i= \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(O_i - E_i) ^ 2}{E_i}$$

## M&M colors

 Color  | Proportion | Expected | Observed | $(O - E)^2 / E$
--------|:----------:|:--------:|:--------:|:---------------:
 Blue   | 0.24       | 50.4     | 43       | `r round((O[1] - E[1]) ^ 2 / E[1], 2)`
 Orange | 0.20       | 42.0     | 40       | `r round((O[2] - E[2]) ^ 2 / E[2], 2)`
 Green  | 0.16       | 33.6     | 37       | `r round((O[3] - E[3]) ^ 2 / E[3], 2)`
 Yellow | 0.14       | 29.4     | 37       | `r round((O[4] - E[4]) ^ 2 / E[4], 2)`

 Brown  | 0.13       | 27.3     | 20       | `r round((O[6] - E[6]) ^ 2 / E[6], 2)`
 **Total**  | 1.00   | 210      | 210      | `r round(sum((O - E) ^ 2 / E), 2)`

::: {.pause-think}
What is the test statistic?

$$\chi^2= \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(O_i - E_i) ^ 2}{E_i} = `r round(sum((O - E) ^ 2 / E), 2)`$$
:::

## &nbsp;

How often would we expect a discrepancy of $\ge `r round(sum((O - E) ^ 2 / E), 2)`$ under $H_0$?

## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}

1. State $H_0$ and $H_\mathrm{A}$
2. Calculate the test statistic
3. **Generate the null distribution**
4. Calculate the $P$-value
6. Decide:
    - Reject $H_0$ if test statistic is $\ge$ critical value ($P \le \alpha$)
    - Fail to reject $H_0$ if test statistic is < critical value ($P > \alpha$)

## [$\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert}

> The **[$\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert}** is the sampling distribution for $\chi^2$ test statistic

**Assumptions**

* None of the categories should have an expected frequency of less than 1
* No more than 20% of the categories should have expected frequencies less than 5

## [$\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert}

> The **[$\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert}** is the sampling distribution for $\chi^2$ test statistic

Under the null hypothesis, the more categories, the larger the test statistic

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**3 categories**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\chi^2 &= \sum_{i=1}^3 \frac{(O_i - E_i) ^ 2}{E_i} \\
&= \frac{(O_1 - E_1) ^ 2}{E_1} + \frac{(O_2 - E_2) ^ 2}{E_2} + \frac{(O_3 - E_3) ^ 2}{E_3}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**6 categories**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\chi^2 = &\sum_{i=1}^3 \frac{(O_i - E_i) ^ 2}{E_i} \\
= &\frac{(O_1 - E_1) ^ 2}{E_1} + \frac{(O_2 - E_2) ^ 2}{E_2} + \frac{(O_3 - E_3) ^ 2}{E_3} + \\
&\frac{(O_4 - E_4) ^ 2}{E_4} + \frac{(O_5 - E_5) ^ 2}{E_5} + \frac{(O_6 - E_6) ^ 2}{E_6}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
:::

## [Degrees of freedom for $\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert}

> The [degrees of freedom]{.alert} of a $\chi^2$ statistic capture this fact that more categories equates to larger values

$$df = \mathrm{(Number~of~categories)} - 1$$

## M&M colors

 Color  | Proportion | Expected | Observed | $(O - E)^2 / E$
--------|:----------:|:--------:|:--------:|:---------------:
 Blue   | 0.24       | 50.4     | 43       | `r round((O[1] - E[1]) ^ 2 / E[1], 2)`
 Orange | 0.20       | 42.0     | 40       | `r round((O[2] - E[2]) ^ 2 / E[2], 2)`
 Green  | 0.16       | 33.6     | 37       | `r round((O[3] - E[3]) ^ 2 / E[3], 2)`
 Yellow | 0.14       | 29.4     | 37       | `r round((O[4] - E[4]) ^ 2 / E[4], 2)`
 Red    | 0.13       | 27.3     | 33       | `r round((O[5] - E[5]) ^ 2 / E[5], 2)`
 Brown  | 0.13       | 27.3     | 20       | `r round((O[6] - E[6]) ^ 2 / E[6], 2)`
 **Total**  | 1.00   | 210      | 210      | `r round(sum((O - E) ^ 2 / E), 2)`

$$df =  \mathrm{(Number~of~categories)} - 1 $$

$$\mathit{df} = 6 - 1 = 5$$

## $\chi_5^2$ distribution with test statistic

Recall we calculated for the M&Ms: $\chi^2 = 6.63$

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "9.5in"

mm_test_stat <- sum((O - E) ^ 2 / E)

df <- tibble(
  x = seq(0, 20, 0.01),
  y = dchisq(x, 5)
)

gp <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(fill = "tomato") +
  xlab(expression(chi^2~statistic)) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 24),
    title = element_text(size = 24)
  )

gp +
  geom_area(data = filter(df, x < mm_test_stat), fill = "white",
            size = 2, color = "tomato") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mm_test_stat, size = 2)
```

## $\chi_\mathit{df}^2$ distribution

The $P$-value will be the area to the right of test statistic.

So this is a [one-tailed]{.alert} test. Why?

We are only interested if the discrepancy between *Expected* and *Observed* is **more** than we expect under $H_0$

$$\frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i}$$

Higher test statistics = more discrepancy between *Expected* and *Observed*

## [$P$-value]{.alert}

$\chi^2~\text{statistic} = `r sum((O - E) ^ 2 / E)`$, $\mathit{df} = 5$

```{r}
#| echo: true

pchisq(q = 6.632544,
       df = 5,
       lower.tail = FALSE)
```

## Learning Objectives

1. Understand [odds ratios]{.alert}, their connection to [contingency analysis]{.alert}, and their confidence intervals
2. Gain appreciation for missuses of $P$-values and the partial solution offered by confidence intervals
3. Gain appreciation for the role of racism, eugenics, and personal bias (not statistical bias) in foundational statistics

## Review: [$\chi^2$ statistic]{.alert}

> The [$\chi^2$]{.alert} statistic measures the discrepency between observed frequencies from the data and expected frequencies from the null hypothesis

[$\chi^2$ statistic]{.alert} is calculated by summing up all $n$ $\chi^2_i$ values

$$\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \chi^2_i= \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(O_i - E_i) ^ 2}{E_i}$$

## Review: [$\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert}

> The **[$\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert}** is the sampling distribution for $\chi^2$ test statistic

**Assumptions**

* None of the categories should have an expected frequency of less than 1
* No more than 20% of the categories should have expected frequencies less than 5

## [$\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert}

> The **[$\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert}** is the sampling distribution for $\chi^2$ test statistic

Under the null hypothesis, the more categories, the larger the test statistic

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**3 categories**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\chi^2 &= \sum_{i=1}^3 \frac{(O_i - E_i) ^ 2}{E_i} \\
&= \frac{(O_1 - E_1) ^ 2}{E_1} + \frac{(O_2 - E_2) ^ 2}{E_2} + \frac{(O_3 - E_3) ^ 2}{E_3}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**6 categories**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\chi^2 = &\sum_{i=1}^3 \frac{(O_i - E_i) ^ 2}{E_i} \\
= &\frac{(O_1 - E_1) ^ 2}{E_1} + \frac{(O_2 - E_2) ^ 2}{E_2} + \frac{(O_3 - E_3) ^ 2}{E_3} + \\
&\frac{(O_4 - E_4) ^ 2}{E_4} + \frac{(O_5 - E_5) ^ 2}{E_5} + \frac{(O_6 - E_6) ^ 2}{E_6}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
:::

## [Degrees of freedom for $\chi^2$ distribution]{.alert}

> The [degrees of freedom]{.alert} of a $\chi^2$ statistic capture this fact that more categories equates to larger values

**For goodness of fit test:** $df = \mathrm{(Number~of~categories)} - 1$

**For contingency analysis:** $df = (\mathrm{Number~of~rows} - 1) \times (\mathrm{Number~of~columns} - 1)$

## Contingency analysis

|                       | **Contingency test**  |
|-----------------------|-----------------------|
| Number of variables   | **2**                 |
| Type of data          | categorical  |
| Parameter             | *Odds ratio (OR)*  |
| Estimate              | $\hat{OR}$  |
| Sampling distribution | $\chi^2$ distribution |
| Test statistic        | $\chi^2$ statistic    |

The [odds ratio]{.alert} is the fraction of how likely a certain outcome is in one group compared to the other

## Odds and odds ratio

[Odds]{.alert} describes how likely, e.g., C-section is compared to vaginal birth

$$
\text{Odds(C-section)} = \frac{Pr(\text{C-section})}{Pr(\text{vaginal birth})}
$$

If the [odds]{.alert} are equal to 1, both outcomes are equally probable

## Odds and odds ratio

[Odds ratio]{.alert} compares the odds of an outcome, e.g., C-section, across different groups

(note: only works for `2 x 2` contingency tables)

$$
\text{OR} = \frac{\text{Odds(C-section for non-English speakers)}}{\text{Odds(C-section for English speakers)}}
$$

If the [odds ratio]{.alert} is equal to 1, both groups have the same odds

**Our null hypothesis is that the odds ratio is equal to 1**

## Odds and odds ratio

The [odds ratio]{.alert} we calculate from data is an estimate $\hat{OR}$

|                            | non-English speaker | English speaker |
|---------------------------:|:--------------------|:----------------|
| Primary Caesarean delivery | 127                 | 934             |
| Primary vaginal delivery   | 1022                | 9336            |
| Odds $\hat{O}$             | 127/1022            | 934/9336 |

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat{OR} &= \frac{\hat{O}_{nE}}{\hat{O}_{E}} \\
&= \frac{127/1022}{934/9336} \\
&= 1.242
\end{aligned}
$$

## Odds and odds ratio

The [odds ratio]{.alert} we calculate from data is an estimate $\hat{OR}$

|                            | non-English speaker | English speaker |
|---------------------------:|:--------------------|:----------------|
| Primary Caesarean delivery | 127                 | 934             |
| Primary vaginal delivery   | 1022                | 9336            |
| Odds $\hat{O}$             | 127/1022            | 934/9336 |

$$
\hat{OR} = 1.242
$$

**Our null hypothesis is that the odds ratio is equal to 1**

Null hypothesis test: *Is 1.242 significantly different from 1?*

- $P$-value
- or...

## Confidence interval for the odds ratio

**95% CI**

- the range of values that contain 95% of the central probability of the sampling distribution for the estimate
- the range will overlap the *true population parameter* 95% of the time in hypothetical repeat studies
- if the 95% CI does not overlap the null hypothesis (e.g. $OR = 1$) we reject the null at $\alpha = 0.05$
- confidence intervals give us more information that $P$-values alone

## Confidence interval for the odds ratio

The **95% CI** for the natural log of the odds ratio follows the nice (approximate) rule

$$
\text{95\% CI} = \ln(\hat{OR}) \pm 2 \times SE_\text{log-scale}
$$

An even better approximation is

$$
\text{95\% CI} = \ln(\hat{OR}) \pm 1.96 \times SE_\text{log-scale}
$$

## Confidence interval for the odds ratio

$$
\text{95\% CI} = \ln(\hat{OR}) \pm 1.96 \times SE_\text{log-scale}
$$

But what is $SE_\text{log-scale}$?  Just take my word for it:

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
|              | group 1 | group 2 |
|-------------:|:----------------|:----------------|
| response 1 | a               | c             |
| response 2 | b               | d            |
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
$$
SE_\text{log-scale} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c} + \frac{1}{d}}
$$
:::
:::

## Confidence interval for the odds ratio

|                            | non-English speaker | English speaker |
|---------------------------:|:--------------------|:----------------|
| Primary Caesarean delivery | 127                 | 934             |
| Primary vaginal delivery   | 1022                | 9336            |

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{95\% CI} &= \ln(\hat{OR}) \pm 1.96 \times SE_\text{log-scale} \\
&= \ln(1.242) \pm 1.96 \times \sqrt{\frac{1}{127} + \frac{1}{1022} + \frac{1}{934} + \frac{1}{9336}} \\
&= \ln(1.242) \pm 1.96 \times 0.100 \\
&= \ln(1.242) \pm 0.196
\end{aligned}
$$

## Confidence interval for the odds ratio

|                            | non-English speaker | English speaker |
|---------------------------:|:--------------------|:----------------|
| Primary Caesarean delivery | 127                 | 934             |
| Primary vaginal delivery   | 1022                | 9336            |

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{95\% CI} &= \ln(\hat{OR}) \pm 1.96 \times SE_\text{log-scale} \\
&= \ln(1.242) \pm 0.196
\end{aligned}
$$

```{r}
#| echo: true

ci95logLo <- log(1.242) - 0.196
ci95logHi <- log(1.242) + 0.196

# convert back to linear (not log) measurements
exp(c(ci95logLo, ci95logHi))
```

## $\chi^2$ contingency tests are all approximate

Here is a more accurate what of getting all the same information:

```{r}
#| echo: true

# make the contingency table in R
d <- matrix(c(127, 1022, 934, 9336), nrow = 2)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# an "exact" test without the chi-sqrd assumptions
fisher.test(d)
```

## $\chi^2$ contingency tests are all approximate

Here is a more accurate what of getting all the same information:

```{r}
#| echo: true

fisher.test(d)
```

## Why do we care so much about [confidence intervals]{.alert}?

**There's a replication crisis in biostatistics**

- Studies will publish a "significant" finding (one with $P$-value $\le 0.05$)
- Other researchers will try to reproduce that finding, and more often than not, **they fail**
- Are any of our insights valid?!

[Blakeley et al. (2019)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00031305.2018.1527253) write about this problem in an article titled:

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
*Abandon Statistical Significance*
:::

(i.e. no more $P$-values, please)

## Why do we care so much about [confidence intervals]{.alert}?

**There's a replication crisis in biostatistics**

Confidence intervals are a small, simple, incomplete fix: they let us keep doing statistics pretty much the same, but CIs are *more informative* and thus less prone to *P-hacking*

## Why do we care so much about [confidence intervals]{.alert}?

**There's a replication crisis in biostatistics**

Confidence intervals are a small, simple, incomplete fix

An example with odds ratios (the null hypothesis is $OR = 1$)

| $P$-value | $\chi^2$ stat | odds ratio | (95% CI) |
|-----------|---------------|------------|----------|
| $P = 0.01$ | 6.63 | 1.211 | (1.011, 1.425) |
| $P = 0.01$ | 6.63 | 1.003 | (1.001, 1.004) |
| $P = 0.01$ | 6.63 | 2.327 | (1.983, 3.782) |

$P$-values are all the same, but due to different sample sizes and true effect sizes, odds ratios and confidence intervals are wildly different, with some warranting our interest and others not

## Why do we care so much about [confidence intervals]{.alert}?

**There's a replication crisis in biostatistics**

Confidence intervals are a small, simple, incomplete fix

An example with odds ratios (the null hypothesis is $OR = 1$)

| $P$-value | $\chi^2$ stat | odds ratio | (95% CI) | conclusion |
|-----------|---------------|------------|----------|------------|
| $P = 0.01$ | 6.63 | 1.211 | (1.011, 1.425) | Could be interesting, needs more samples |
| $P = 0.01$ | 6.63 | 1.003 | (1.001, 1.004) | Huge sample size, biologically meaningless |
| $P = 0.01$ | 6.63 | 2.327 | (1.983, 3.782) | Clearly there's an effect |
